label: Topology of Surfaces
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 379 through 395 and turns closed surfaces into inspectable invariants. We meet the Euler characteristic, the polygon-with-edges-identified picture, orientability, the classification of all closed surfaces, and finally the bridge to geometry through the Gauss-Bonnet theorem connecting curvature to topology.

label: Euler Characteristic
notes: For any polyhedral subdivision of a surface the alternating count V minus E plus F is a topological invariant: refining or distorting the mesh never changes it. The sphere gives two, so every convex polyhedron satisfies Euler's celebrated relation. This single number organizes the entire chapter.

label: Invariance Under Subdivision
notes: Why is the Euler characteristic invariant? Each elementary move that refines a subdivision leaves V minus E plus F unchanged. Splitting a face adds one edge and one face; splitting an edge adds one vertex and one edge. Because the moves cancel, any two subdivisions of the same surface agree.

label: Fundamental Polygon
notes: Every closed surface is a polygon whose boundary edges are glued in pairs, recorded by a word in symbols and inverses. Reading the word tells us the gluing arrows. This combinatorial scheme replaces hard three-dimensional pictures with a flat diagram that we can compute on directly.

label: The Torus aba^{-1}b^{-1}
notes: Gluing the opposite sides of a square with matching arrows yields a torus, encoded by the word a b a inverse b inverse. All four corners become one vertex, the two edge pairs give two edges, and the single square is one face, so V minus E plus F equals zero.

label: Projective Plane and Klein Bottle
notes: Changing the gluing word changes the surface. The word a a builds the projective plane with characteristic one; a b a b builds the Klein bottle with characteristic zero. Both contain reversed-arrow identifications, the signature of non-orientability that distinguishes them from the torus.

label: The Mobius Band
notes: The Mobius band is the elementary non-orientable surface: a strip glued with a half twist. It has only one side and one boundary curve, and a normal arrow carried once around returns reversed. Every non-orientable closed surface contains a Mobius band as a cross-cap.

label: Orientability as Transport
notes: Orientability is a transport test. Carry a small local frame once around a loop; on an orientable surface like the torus it returns compatible, dot product plus one, while on a Mobius-type strip it returns mirror reversed, dot product minus one. That sign cleanly separates the two surface classes.

label: Classification of Surfaces
notes: The classification theorem is the chapter's summit. Every closed orientable surface is a sphere with g handles and has characteristic two minus twice g. Every closed non-orientable surface is a connected sum of projective planes, a sphere carrying cross-caps. Genus and orientability are a complete pair of invariants.

label: Genus and Connected Sums
notes: Adding a handle to a surface lowers the characteristic by two; adding a cross-cap lowers it by one. These two moves generate every closed surface from the sphere. The genus counts handles, so the orientable family marches two two zero negative-two as we attach more handles.

label: Gauss-Bonnet Bridge
notes: Geometry meets topology in Gauss-Bonnet: the total Gaussian curvature integrated over a closed surface equals two pi times its Euler characteristic. Bend and stretch the surface however you like; the curvature redistributes but its integral is pinned by the topology. Curvature cannot escape the characteristic.

label: Recap and Coloring Coda
notes: We recap the chapter's shared currency, the Euler characteristic, spent by handles, cross-caps, and gluing words alike. As a coda, Euler's formula forces a low-degree face, giving the six-color theorem on the sphere, while Heawood's number bounds colors on every other surface, with the Klein bottle as the famous exception.
